pr_title: Change Request connection logic to try both IPv6 and IPv4 when available

issue_context.title: Problem running on an IPv6-only server
issue_context.body:
### Steps to reproduce the problem

1. Install Mastodon on a system that has no IPv4 addresses
2. Attempt to search for someone on a server that has both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses


### Expected behaviour

The user should be found and displayed in the search results

### Actual behaviour

Error "503 Remote data could not be fetched" is displayed for some servers, but not for others

### Detailed description

To try to diagnose this, I edited `app/controllers/api/base_controller.rb` to return the exception`.as_s` instead of "Remote data could not be fetched". It appears that Mastodon is trying to connect to an IPv4 address, even though there are both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses for the remote server in the DNS.

I'm suspicious about this line: https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/blob/bb89f83cc06b9665205c62db21163f2ce43d97ed/app/lib/request.rb#L196

_Why_ are only the first two addresses looked up in the DNS being used? Many servers have more than two addresses; for example, mastodon.scot has two IPv4 and two IPv6 addresses. The `take(2)` appears to originate in commit fd8145d2322d8b13b6aaa9cd2a61331ff660c9dd but there's no rationale provided for it.

I don't think the addresses are guaranteed to be returned in any particular order? My guess is that, for some servers, the first two addresses returned happen to be IPv4 addresses and the IPv6 addresses aren't being tried at all.

If I remove the `take(2)` then the problem appears to be fixed for me.

### Specifications

Mastodon 3.5.3
comments:
I suspect the `take(2)` is to avoid doing lots of work for servers that have many addresses.

So, rather than removing it entirely, I think the correct fix is going to be to take the first _n_ addresses of each address type.
Similar problem - https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/issues/15795

> I suspect the `take(2)` is to avoid doing lots of work for servers that have many addresses.

Yes, as far as I can guess and remember, this is the reason.

> So, rather than removing it entirely, I think the correct fix is going to be to take the first _n_ addresses of each address type.

That makes sense to me, and since we are opening connections concurrently in that part, the performance impact shouldn't be too bad.
I just migrated my mastodon instance to a new server with ipv6 only (old one had both) and can confirm this problem too.

The only other issue I had on an IPv6-only server was needing to add the NAT64 address range (for connections to IPv4-only servers, typically something like `64:ff9b::/96`) to `ALLOWED_PRIVATE_ADDRESSES` in `.env.production` — without that, _all_ connections to IPv4-only servers would fail.
@solick it actually is documented here: https://docs.joinmastodon.org/admin/config/#allowed-private-addresses
I think the best solution here would be a proper [Happy Eyeballs](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8305) implementation.

@ClearlyClaire thanks for hinting me to the correct config. I was wondering if this parameter means the local bind addresses our what exactly is meant with allowed-private-addresses? So I would bind to the servers ipv6 and ipv4 upstream address in the config?

> @ClearlyClaire thanks for hinting me to the correct config. I was wondering if this parameter means the local bind addresses our what exactly is meant with allowed-private-addresses? So I would bind to the servers ipv6 and ipv4 upstream address in the config?

I don't know if you need to use this environment variable, but @sde1000 used it so that Mastodon accepted accessing their NAT64 addresses. If you use that, you probably need to use `ALLOWED_PRIVATE_ADDRESSES` to list your NAT64 prefix

@solick No, it's nothing to do with local socket addresses.

By default Mastodon won't connect out to addresses it considers to be "private". In IPv4 world this is ranges like 192.168/16, 10/8, 172.16/12 — not globally routed, typically used behind NAT for private networks.

This is a sensible policy because it prevents a Mastodon installation being used to probe services on its local network that ought not to be exposed to the internet at large.

Some IPv6 address ranges are considered to be "private" too. Similar criteria: not globally routed, typically used for private networks. The complete list is at https://github.com/jtdowney/private_address_check/blob/main/lib/private_address_check.rb and includes the range usually used for NAT64.

NAT64 is a way to allow systems that only have IPv6 connectivity to make connections to IPv4 addresses. The router, which does have IPv4 connectivity, is configured such that part of the IPv6 address space (typically 64:ff9b::/96, although other ranges can be used) is translated to IPv4 addresses. Eg. the router would translate IPv6 packets addressed to 64:ff9b::102:304 into IPv4 packets addressed to 1.2.3.4 and manage the reverse translation in exactly the same way that NAT works in the IPv4 world.

So if your Mastodon installation _only_ has IPv6 connectivity, and relies on NAT64 for access to the IPv4 world, you may need to add its NAT64 prefix to ALLOWED_PRIVATE_ADDRESSES if you find that it can't connect to IPv4-only instances.

To find its NAT64 prefix, do a DNS lookup for a system that only has IPv4 addresses (for example mastodon.social, at the moment). You should find that the DNS server has been configured to invent suitable AAAA records with the appropriate NAT64 prefix. For example, if I look up mastodon.social on the system running my Mastodon installation, I see:

```
steve@bag:~$ host mastodon.social
mastodon.social has address 136.243.102.156
mastodon.social has IPv6 address 64:ff9b::88f3:669c
mastodon.social mail is handled by 50 mx3.zoho.eu.
mastodon.social mail is handled by 20 mx2.zoho.eu.
mastodon.social mail is handled by 10 mx.zoho.eu.
```

@sde1000 thanks for explanation, I don't use NAT64 instead I use a linux bridge with IPv4 upstream. I can ping mastodon.social without problems but host mastodon.socail don't show a IPv6 address at all.
